name: ATTINY461A-XU
title: ATtiny261A/461A/861A 8-bit AVR microcontrollers with 2/4/8 Kbytes in-system programmable Flash
summary: Three low-power 8-bit AVR RISC microcontrollers that execute most of their 123 instructions in a single clock, reaching 20 MIPS at 20 MHz from 4.5 V to 5.5 V and running down to 1.8 V at 4 MHz. The three devices carry 2, 4 or 8 Kbytes of self-programmable Flash with 128, 256 or 512 bytes each of EEPROM and SRAM. On chip are an 8/16-bit timer, a high-speed 8/10-bit timer with three PWM outputs, dead-time generation and a 64 MHz PLL clock, a 10-bit ADC with 11 single-ended inputs and 16 differential pairs (15 with 1x/8x/20x/32x gain), an analog comparator, the USI serial interface, a watchdog with its own oscillator, a calibrated 8 MHz RC oscillator, a temperature sensor and 16 I/O lines with pin-change interrupts. ATTINY461A-XU is the 4 Kbyte device in the 20-lead TSSOP for -40 °C to 85 °C.

operation.text: Low-power CMOS 8-bit parts on the AVR enhanced RISC core. With most instructions taking one clock, throughput comes close to 1 MIPS per MHz. All 32 working registers feed the ALU directly, so one instruction can read two registers and complete in one cycle.

Each device has its Flash (2/4/8 Kbytes), EEPROM and SRAM (128/256/512 bytes each), 16 general purpose I/O lines, 32 working registers, an 8-bit timer with compare modes, a high-speed 8-bit timer, the USI, interrupts from inside and outside, a 10-bit ADC with 11 channels, a watchdog with its own oscillator and four software-selected sleep modes. Flash can be rewritten in-system over SPI, by an ordinary non-volatile memory programmer, or by boot code running on the core.
Qualification projects a retention failure rate well under 1 PPM over 20 years at 85°C, or over 100 years at 25°C.

Harvard architecture: program and data memories sit on separate buses. A one-stage pipeline fetches the next instruction while the present one executes, so an instruction can finish on every clock. The 32 x 8-bit register file has single-cycle access; six of its registers pair up as the 16-bit X, Y and Z pointers for indirect data addressing, and Z can also address lookup tables in Flash. Most instructions are one 16-bit word; every program address holds a 16- or 32-bit instruction. Jumps and calls reach the whole address space. The I/O space holds 64 addresses, reachable directly or as data addresses 0x20 - 0x5F.

The ALU performs arithmetic, logic and bit operations between two registers, or between a register and a constant, in one clock. SREG reflects the outcome of the latest arithmetic instruction and is updated after every ALU operation. It is not saved on interrupt entry or restored on return; software has to do that. SREG bits: I global interrupt enable (cleared by hardware on an interrupt, set by RETI, also set and cleared with SEI and CLI), T bit-copy storage for BLD/BST, H half carry, S sign (N exclusive-or V), V two's complement overflow, N negative, Z zero, C carry.

Registers R0 to R31 also occupy data addresses 0x00 to 0x1F, so the X, Y and Z pointers can index any register. X is R27:R26, Y is R29:R28 and Z is R31:R30 (high:low). The file supports one or two 8-bit operands with an 8-bit result, two 8-bit operands with a 16-bit result, and a 16-bit operand with a 16-bit result. The pointers can auto-increment and auto-decrement in some addressing modes.

The stack is in SRAM and grows toward lower addresses. Software must set SP above the start of SRAM before any call or enabled interrupt; after reset SP holds the last SRAM address (RAMEND). SP is two 8-bit I/O registers, SPH and SPL; on parts whose data space is small enough, SPH is absent.
The CPU runs on clkCPU, taken straight from the selected clock source with no internal division. In one clock an ALU instruction fetches two register operands, executes and writes the result back.

The reset and each interrupt have their own vector at the bottom of program memory; a lower vector address means higher priority, RESET first and INT0 next. Each interrupt has its own enable bit, which works only with the global I bit set. Entering an interrupt clears I, and RETI sets it again; software may set I inside a handler to allow nesting. Flag-type interrupts set a flag that hardware clears on vectoring, or software clears by writing one; a flag set while disabled is kept until served. Level-type interrupts fire only while their condition lasts. After a return one more main-program instruction executes before a pending interrupt is served. CLI takes effect at once, even against an interrupt arriving on the same cycle; after SEI the next instruction executes before any pending interrupt.

At least four clocks pass from an interrupt to the first instruction at its vector, during which the PC is pushed; the jump at the vector takes three more clocks. A multi-cycle instruction in progress completes first. Waking from sleep adds four clocks to the response, on top of the sleep mode's start-up time. Returning from a handler takes four clocks: the two-byte PC is popped, SP rises by two and I is set.

2/4/8 Kbytes of in-system reprogrammable Flash, organised as 1024/2048/4096 x 16 because every instruction is 16 or 32 bits. It survives at least 10,000 write/erase cycles. The PC is 10/11/12 bits wide. Constant tables may sit anywhere in program memory and are read with LPM.

The data space starts with the 32 registers, then 64 I/O registers, then 128/256/512 bytes of SRAM. Five addressing modes reach it: direct (whole data space), indirect with displacement (63 locations from the Y or Z base), indirect, and indirect with pre-decrement or post-increment.
An SRAM access takes two clkCPU cycles.

128/256/512 bytes of EEPROM in a separate data space, read and written a byte at a time, rated for at least 100,000 write/erase cycles. Its address, data and control registers sit in I/O space. A read stalls the CPU for four clocks; a write stalls it for two. A self-timing flag tells software when the next byte may be written; writes follow a set procedure so that stray writes do not happen.

Atomic mode (EEPMn = 00): with the address in EEAR and data in EEDR, setting EEPE within four cycles of EEMPE erases and writes in one operation. Split mode separates the two: EEPMn = 01 erases only and EEPMn = 10 writes only, so time-critical moments can use the shorter write once the location was erased earlier; writing to a location not first erased loses the data. EEPE stays set until the operation ends, and no other EEPROM operation is possible meanwhile. EEPROM timing comes from the calibrated oscillator, so its frequency must stay within the OSCCAL limits.

Too low a VCC can corrupt EEPROM data in two ways: the write sequence itself needs a minimum voltage, and the CPU may execute instructions wrongly. Holding the part in reset through low-supply periods prevents both, using the internal brown-out detector or, where its threshold does not fit, an external low-VCC reset circuit. A write in progress when reset occurs still completes if the supply is high enough.

Every I/O and peripheral register is in I/O space, reachable with LD/LDS/LDD and ST/STS/STD. Registers at 0x00 - 0x1F are bit-accessible with SBI and CBI and testable with SBIS and SBIC. IN and OUT use I/O addresses 0x00 - 0x3F; LD and ST use those addresses plus 0x20. Reserved bits should be written as zero and reserved addresses never written. Some status flags clear when written with one; CBI and SBI touch only the named bit, so they are safe on such registers. Three general purpose I/O registers are free for global variables and flags.

clkCPU runs the core: register file, SREG and the stack pointer's data memory. clkI/O runs most I/O modules such as the timers and the external interrupt module, though some external interrupts are detected asynchronously and work with clkI/O stopped. clkFLASH runs the Flash interface, usually together with clkCPU. clkADC is a separate domain so that the CPU and I/O clocks can be stopped during conversions for less noise. clkPCK is a fast peripheral clock from the on-chip PLL that can run faster than the core; the PLL can also provide a prescaled system clock. Unused clocks can be stopped by the sleep modes.

The CKSEL fuses pick the clock source. On wake-up from power-down or power-save the chosen source times the start-up so the oscillator is stable before code runs. From reset an extra delay, timed by the watchdog oscillator, lets the supply settle first.

With CKSEL = 0000 the part runs from a clock applied to CLKI; the SUT fuses set the start-up times. The applied frequency must not change suddenly: a cycle-to-cycle step above 2% can cause unpredictable behaviour, so hold the part in reset across such steps. The system clock prescaler gives run-time frequency changes instead.

The internal PLL multiplies the internal 8 MHz oscillator by eight, giving a 64 MHz fast peripheral clock clkPCK by default. clkPCK can clock Timer/Counter1, and the PLL output divided by four (16 MHz) can be the system clock, chosen with CKSEL = 0001; the PLL runs when CKSEL is 0001 and PLLE in PLLCSR is set. The internal oscillator and PLL are off in power-down and standby. Setting LSM in PLLCSR feeds the PLL from the oscillator divided by two, halving clkPCK to 32 MHz; LSM cannot be set while the PLL clocks the system. Since the PLL tracks the oscillator, changing OSCCAL changes clkPCK; raised well above 8 MHz, clkPCK saturates near 85 MHz and loses lock, so OSCCAL should keep the oscillator at or below 8 MHz. PLOCK in PLLCSR reads one when the PLL is locked.

About 8 MHz with no external parts, selected with CKSEL = 0010; it varies with voltage and temperature but can be calibrated closely by the user. Reset loads the factory calibration value into OSCCAL. Parts leave the factory with CKDIV8 programmed. Writing OSCCAL from software can give better accuracy than the factory calibration. The watchdog oscillator still times the watchdog and the reset time-out when this oscillator clocks the part.
A low-power 128 kHz oscillator, selected with CKSEL = 0011; its frequency depends on supply, temperature and batch.

For a 32.768 kHz watch crystal, selected with CKSEL = 0100 and wired as the crystal connection. Suitable capacitors come from the crystal's own datasheet; the oscillator itself adds internal load capacitance on each pin.

XTAL1 is the input and XTAL2 the output of an inverting amplifier that forms the on-chip oscillator with a quartz crystal or a ceramic resonator. C1 and C2 are always equal; the best value depends on the crystal or resonator, stray capacitance and the noise around it. CKSEL[3:1] chooses one of the frequency ranges; CKSEL0 with SUT[1:0] chooses the start-up time.

Shipped with CKSEL = 0010, SUT = 10 and CKDIV8 programmed: the internal 8 MHz oscillator with the longest start-up, divided by 8. Unprogramming CKDIV8 can overclock the part, since at low supply its rating is below the internal oscillator frequency.

CLKPR divides the system clock to save power when less speed is needed. It works with every clock source and divides clkI/O, clkADC, clkCPU and clkFLASH. Changing the setting produces no glitches and no intermediate frequency above either the old or the new one. The prescaler is a ripple counter on the undivided clock, so the exact switching time cannot be predicted. CLKPS can be changed only by first writing CLKPCE to one with the other bits zero; hardware clears CLKPCE four cycles later or when CLKPS is written.

With the CKOUT fuse programmed the system clock (after the prescaler) appears on CLKO, overriding the pin's I/O function, when the pin is not used as XTAL2. The clock is output with the internal RC oscillator, the watchdog oscillator, the PLL or an external clock, but not with a crystal oscillator.

OSCCAL trims the calibrated internal oscillator: 0x00 gives the lowest frequency and 0xFF the highest. Reset loads the factory value; software may rewrite it within the range given in the electrical characteristics, outside of which calibration is not guaranteed. EEPROM and Flash write timing comes from this oscillator, so do not calibrate above 8.8 MHz when writing them, or the write may fail.

Setting SE in MCUCR and executing SLEEP enters the mode chosen by SM[1:0]: 00 Idle, 01 ADC Noise Reduction, 10 Power-down, 11 Standby. An enabled interrupt wakes the part, which halts four cycles beyond the start-up time, runs the handler and continues after the SLEEP instruction; registers and SRAM are kept. A reset during sleep wakes the part to the reset vector. A level interrupt used for wake-up must be held long enough for the part to wake and enter the handler. Writing SE just before SLEEP and clearing it on wake-up avoids entering sleep by accident.

Stops clkCPU and clkFLASH; the analog comparator, ADC, timers, watchdog and interrupt system keep running, and internal as well as external interrupts can wake the part. Setting ACD in ACSR powers down the comparator when it is not needed for wake-up. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry.

Stops clkI/O, clkCPU and clkFLASH while the ADC, watchdog and external interrupts keep running, giving the ADC a quieter environment. An enabled ADC starts a conversion on entry. Wake-up sources: ADC conversion complete, external reset, watchdog reset, brown-out reset, SPM/EEPROM ready, a level interrupt on INT0, or a pin change.

Stops the oscillator and every generated clock; only asynchronous modules run. The external interrupts and watchdog continue if enabled. Wake-up sources: external reset, watchdog reset, brown-out reset, a level interrupt on INT0, or a pin change.
Available with a crystal or resonator clock: like power-down but with the oscillator left running, so the part wakes in six clock cycles.

With the BOD enabled by the BODLEVEL fuses, software can switch it off during power-down and standby, bringing sleep current down to the fuse-disabled level. The BOD turns off on entering sleep and back on at wake-up, which then takes about 60 µs so the BOD is working before code continues. To set BODS, write BODS and BODSE both to one, then within four clocks write BODS to one and BODSE to zero; BODS takes effect three clocks later, SLEEP must execute while it is active, and it clears itself after three clocks. The default is BODS = 0, BOD active.

PRR stops the clock to individual peripherals in active and idle modes. A stopped peripheral freezes its state and its I/O registers cannot be read or written; resources it holds stay held, so disable the peripheral before stopping it. Clearing the bit restarts it in the state it had. In the other sleep modes these clocks are already stopped.

Use sleep as much as possible, choose the deepest mode that keeps what is needed, and disable unused functions. Analog comparator: disable it in idle when unused and always in ADC noise reduction; other modes disable it automatically unless it uses the internal reference, in which case disable it in every mode. ADC: it stays on in every sleep mode if enabled; the first conversion after re-enabling is an extended one. Brown-out detector and watchdog: when enabled they run in every sleep mode and contribute markedly to deep-sleep current. Internal reference: on whenever the BOD, comparator or ADC needs it, and needs its start-up time after being turned on.

Before sleep, set every pin for least power, above all so that none drives a resistive load. Where clkI/O and clkADC are both stopped the input buffers are off, except those needed for wake-up. An enabled input left floating or near VCC/2 draws excess current; analog inputs should always have their digital buffers disabled through DIDR0 and DIDR1, since even in active mode a level near VCC/2 draws significant current.

During reset all I/O registers take their initial values and the ports go to their reset state at once, needing no clock; execution then starts at the reset vector, which must hold an RJMP to the reset routine. When no interrupt is ever enabled, program code may occupy the vector locations. After every reset source goes inactive, a delay counter set by the SUT and CKSEL fuses stretches the internal reset so the supply can settle.

Four: power-on reset while VCC is below VPOT; external reset from a low on RESET longer than the minimum pulse; watchdog reset when the enabled watchdog period expires; brown-out reset while VCC is below VBOT with the BOD enabled.

An on-chip detector holds the part in reset while VCC is below its level, both at start-up and on a supply failure. Crossing the threshold starts the delay counter that sets how long reset lasts after VCC rises; reset reasserts with no delay when VCC falls below the level. RESET may be tied to VCC or held low externally for longer.

A low on RESET, when enabled, longer than the minimum pulse width resets the part even with no clock; shorter pulses may not. When the rising edge passes VRST, the delay counter starts the part after tTOUT.

The BOD compares VCC with a level set by the BODLEVEL fuses, with hysteresis. Falling below VBOT- asserts reset at once; rising above VBOT+ starts the part after tTOUT. A dip must last longer than tBOD to be detected.
A watchdog time-out produces a one-CK reset pulse; its falling edge starts the tTOUT delay.

A bandgap reference serves brown-out detection and may feed the analog comparator or the ADC; it varies with supply and temperature. It is on only while the BOD is enabled by the BODLEVEL fuses, ACBG connects it to the comparator, or the ADC is enabled. With the BOD off, allow the reference its start-up time after setting ACBG or enabling the ADC before using their results. Avoiding all three conditions turns the reference off in power-down.

Clocked from its own 128 kHz oscillator, with a prescaler offering ten time-out periods from 2K to 1024K oscillator cycles. WDR restarts it, as do disabling it and any device reset. On expiry without a WDR the part resets to the reset vector; it can instead raise an interrupt, useful for waking from power-down. The WDTON fuse sets one of two safety levels against accidental disabling or period changes.

Safety level 1 (WDTON unprogrammed): the watchdog starts disabled and WDE can be set freely; to disable it, write WDCE and WDE both to one in one operation, then within four clocks write WDE and WDP as wanted with WDCE cleared. Safety level 2 (WDTON programmed): the watchdog is always on and WDE reads one; to change the period, write WDCE and WDE to one, then within four clocks write WDP with WDCE cleared, the value of WDE not mattering.

Nineteen vectors at word addresses 0x0000 to 0x0012, one word apiece, each normally holding an RJMP to its handler; the main program can start at 0x0013. Unused vectors may hold program code when those interrupts are never enabled.

INT0, INT1 and the sixteen PCINT pins raise external interrupts, even when the pins are outputs, which allows software interrupts. A pin change interrupt fires when any PCINT pin enabled in PCMSK toggles; it is detected asynchronously and can wake the part from sleep modes beyond idle. INT0 and INT1 trigger on a falling edge, rising edge or low level as set in MCUCR; a level interrupt keeps triggering while the pin is low. Edge detection needs the I/O clock.

A low level on INT0 is detected asynchronously, so it can wake the part from modes where the I/O clock is stopped. For wake-up from power-down, the level must last until the start-up time ends; if it goes away sooner the part still wakes but no interrupt is taken, and execution resumes after SLEEP.

ISC01:ISC00 in MCUCR choose what on INT0 or INT1 requests an interrupt. The pin is sampled before edge detection: an edge or toggle pulse longer than one clock period always triggers, shorter ones may not. A low-level request must be held until the current instruction completes. GIMSK holds the INT1, INT0, PCIE1 and PCIE0 enables, active together with the I bit in SREG.

All ports offer true read-modify-write as digital I/O: SBI and CBI change one pin's direction, output value or pull-up without touching the others. Outputs drive symmetrically with strong sink and source, enough to drive LED displays directly. Every pin has a selectable pull-up whose resistance does not vary with supply, and protection diodes to VCC and ground. Each port has three I/O addresses: PORTx (data), DDRx (direction) and PINx (input, read only); writing one to a PINx bit toggles the PORTx bit. PUD in MCUCR disables every pull-up. Enabling an alternate function on some pins leaves the rest of the port usable as general I/O.

DDxn = 1 makes the pin an output, 0 an input. An input with PORTxn = 1 has its pull-up on; clearing PORTxn or making the pin an output switches it off. An output drives high with PORTxn = 1 and low with PORTxn = 0. Pins go tri-state when reset is active, even with no clock running. Writing one to PINxn toggles PORTxn whatever DDxn holds.

Going between tri-state (00) and output high (11) passes through either pull-up on (01) or output low (10). The pull-up state is normally harmless; where it is not, PUD can disable every pull-up. Moving from an input with pull-up to a low output, or back, passes through tri-state or output high.

PINxn reads the pin whatever DDxn holds, through a latch and register that act as a synchronizer against metastability. An external change reaches PINxn between half and one and a half system clock periods later. To read back a value software has just written, insert a NOP: the delay through the synchronizer is then one clock period.

In power-down, power-save and standby the input to the schmitt trigger is clamped to ground so floating or mid-supply inputs draw no current. Pins enabled as external interrupt inputs, or used by certain alternate functions, are exempt; a pin whose external interrupt is not enabled is clamped too. A high level on an asynchronous interrupt pin set for edge or any-change sensing, with the interrupt not enabled, sets its flag on waking from these modes because the clamp creates the change.

Give unused pins a defined level so floating inputs do not draw current in reset, active and idle modes. The internal pull-up is the simplest choice, but it is off during reset; where reset current matters use an external pull-up or pull-down. Tying an unused pin straight to VCC or GND risks heavy current if it is ever made an output.

Most pins carry alternate functions that can override the pull-up, the output driver, the output value, the port toggle and the digital input enable of the general I/O logic, and that receive the pin's digital input or connect to it in analog. The overriding signals come from the modules that own the functions.

AIN pins: set them as inputs with the pull-up off so the digital port does not disturb the comparator. PA3 as AREF: the pull-up and output driver are off when the pin carries an external reference or the internal reference with an external capacitor. PA1 as DO in USI three-wire mode: the USI data output overrides PORTA1 and drives the pin when DDA1 is set; PORTA1 still enables the pull-up while the pin is an input. PA0 as DI in USI three-wire mode: the normal port function is not overridden, so the pin must be set as an input.

PB7: with RSTDISBL unprogrammed the pin is RESET and cannot be I/O (DDB7, PORTB7 and PINB7 then read 0); with RSTDISBL programmed it is an I/O pin and the part relies on power-on and brown-out reset. With DWEN programmed and the lock bits unprogrammed, the pin becomes the debugWIRE line, a bidirectional open-drain I/O with pull-up. ADC7 to ADC10 on PB4 to PB7 run from the analog supply. PB6 also serves as T0 and INT0. PB5: XTAL2 for the crystal or low-frequency crystal oscillator; CLKO outputs the divided system clock with CKOUT programmed, regardless of PORTB5 and DDB5; OC1D output when set as an output. PB4: XTAL1/CLKI for every clock source except the internal calibrated oscillator; ~OC1D output when set as an output. A pin serving as a clock pin is not available as I/O. PB3: OC1B output when DDB3 is set. PB2: USCK/SCL and ~OC1B output. PB1: DO overrides PORTB1 when DDB1 is set, PORTB1 still enabling the pull-up as an input; OC1A output. PB0: DI needs the pin set as input; SDA; ~OC1A output. Each OC1x pin also carries the PWM output of Timer/Counter1.
Writing PUD in MCUCR to one turns off every port pull-up, even on pins with {DDxn, PORTxn} = 0b01.

A general-purpose timer that works as an 8-bit counter with two output compare units or as a 16-bit counter with one, and has an input capture unit. It offers clear on compare match (auto reload) and four interrupt sources: TOV0, OCF0A, OCF0B and ICF0. TIFR shows the interrupt flags and TIMSK masks each one. TCNT0L, OCR0A and OCR0B are 8-bit registers; in 16-bit mode TCNT0H is added and OCR0A (low byte) and OCR0B (high byte) join into one 16-bit compare register.

CS0[2:0] in TCCR0B select the clock: none (timer stopped), the I/O clock directly (CS0 = 1, the fastest, equal to fCLK_I/O), the prescaler taps fCLK_I/O/8, /64, /256 or /1024, or the T0 pin on its rising (CS0 = 7) or falling (CS0 = 6) edge. The prescaler runs freely whatever the clock select, so with a prescaled clock the first count comes 1 to N+1 system clocks after the timer is enabled, N being the divisor; the prescaler reset (PSR0) can align the timer with program execution.

T0 is sampled every system clock and passed through an edge detector, which adds 2.5 to 3.5 system clocks of delay from an edge on the pin to the counter update. T0 should be stable for at least one system clock when the external clock input is turned on or off, or a false count may occur. Each half period of the external clock must exceed one system clock, so fExtClk < fclk_I/O/2 at 50% duty cycle; allowing for oscillator tolerances, staying below fclk_I/O/2.5 is advised. An external clock cannot be prescaled.

The counter steps up on each timer clock, passes TOP and restarts from BOTTOM; CTC0 in TCCR0A sets the sequence. With CS0[2:0] = 0 the timer stops but the CPU can still read and write TCNT0, and a CPU write takes priority over a clear or count. TOV0 is set when the counter reaches its maximum and can raise an interrupt.

An event on ICP0, or on the analog comparator output when ACIC0 in TCCR0A is set, copies TCNT0 into ICR0 and sets ICF0 on the same system clock; with TICIE0 set this raises an interrupt, and ICF0 clears when the interrupt runs or when one is written to it. ICR0 shares storage with the compare registers: OCR0A is the 8-bit capture register, and in 16-bit capture mode OCR0B is its high byte, leaving no compare unit free. In 8-bit capture mode OCR0B still works as a compare register. Changing the trigger source can cause a capture, so clear ICF0 afterwards. Both sources are sampled like T0; driving the ICP0 port bit from software can trigger a capture.

Setting ICNC0 in TCCR0B filters the capture input: the output changes only when four successive samples agree, which adds four system clocks of delay. It runs from the system clock, untouched by the prescaler.

If ICR0 is not read before the next event, it is overwritten. Read ICR0 as early as possible in the interrupt handler; the worst-case response depends on the longest of the other interrupt handlers. To measure duty cycle, switch the trigger edge right after each read and then clear ICF0 by writing one to it; frequency measurement needs no edge change.

TCNT0 is compared continuously with OCR0A and OCR0B; a match sets OCF0A or OCF0B on the next timer clock (only OCF0A in 16-bit mode) and can raise an interrupt. The flag clears when the interrupt runs or when one is written to it. Any CPU write to TCNT0H/L blocks compare matches in the next timer clock, even with the timer stopped, so OCR0A/B can be set equal to TCNT0 without an interrupt; a value written to TCNT0 that equals OCR0A/B therefore misses that match.

TCW0, ICEN0 and CTC0 choose the mode. Normal 8-bit: TCNT0L counts up to 0xFF and wraps to 0x00, setting TOV0 as it becomes zero, like a ninth bit that is only set; the overflow interrupt clears it, so software can extend the resolution, and the counter may be written at any time. CTC 8-bit: the counter clears when it matches OCR0A, which sets TOP and the resolution; OCF0A can interrupt at each TOP so the handler can change it. There is no double buffering: writing OCR0A below the current count makes the counter run to 0xFF and wrap before the next match, so a TOP near BOTTOM needs care at low prescaling. TOV0 still sets on the MAX to 0x00 step. Normal 16-bit: TCNT0H/L counts to 0xFFFF and wraps, TOV0 acting as a 17th bit. 8-bit and 16-bit input capture modes use the input capture unit.

The timer is synchronous, its clock acting as an enable. TOV0 sets as the count passes from MAX to BOTTOM, with or without the prescaler; OCF0x sets on the timer clock after TCNT0 equals OCR0x; in CTC mode the counter goes from TOP to BOTTOM on the timer clock after the match, when OCF0A sets.

In 16-bit mode TCNT0H/L and OCR0A/B are reached through one shared 8-bit temporary register for the high byte. Write the high byte first: the low-byte write copies both into the 16-bit register in one clock. Read the low byte first: that read loads the high byte into the temporary register. The 16-bit compare register in output compare mode is read without the temporary register, but ICR0 in 16-bit capture mode needs it. Since an interrupt that touches any 16-bit timer register corrupts the temporary register, main code should disable interrupts around a 16-bit access when handlers also use these registers. When several registers share the same high byte, it need only be written once.

A high-speed 10-bit timer that can also run as an 8-bit timer, with three independent output compare units, clear on compare match, glitch-free phase and frequency correct PWM, variable PWM period, synchronous and asynchronous clocking with its own prescaler, a dead-time generator per PWM channel, and a fault protection unit that can disable the PWM pins. Interrupt sources are TOV1, OCF1A, OCF1B, OCF1D and FPF1. In PWM mode it gives three PWMs with non-overlapping true and inverted outputs, clocked at up to 64 MHz; high prescaling suits slow or infrequent timing.

Its maximum clock is 64 MHz. Below 2.7 V supply the low speed mode (LSM in PLLCSR) is recommended, halving the fast peripheral clock to 32 MHz, because the timer cannot run fast enough at low voltage.

TCNT1 and OCR1A to OCR1D are 8-bit registers; the 2-bit TC1H register buffers the two most significant bits of every 10-bit value. Reading a low byte loads its two MSBs into TC1H, and writing a low byte takes the two MSBs from TC1H. With the MSBs written as zero the timer behaves as 8-bit. OCR1A, OCR1B and OCR1D drive OC1A, OC1B and OC1D and their compare interrupts; OCR1C holds TOP, the clear-on-match value. Flags sit in TIFR and TCCR1D, masks in TIMSK and FPIE1 in TCCR1D, control in TCCR1A to TCCR1E.

In asynchronous mode the timer and prescaler run from the fast peripheral clock PCK (64 MHz, or 32 MHz in low speed mode) while the CPU runs from any source, with a synchronization boundary between the two domains. Register writes pass through input synchronization registers before acting on the counter. TCCR1A to TCCR1D and OCR1A to OCR1D read back at once after a write, but TCNT1, TC1H and the flags OCF1A, OCF1B, OCF1D and TOV1 read back late because of input and output synchronization. The system clock must be below half the PCK frequency, since synchronization needs two PCK edges while the system clock is high; a faster system clock risks losing data or control values.

The timer runs from the system clock CK (synchronous mode) or from PCK (asynchronous mode, chosen by PCKE in PLLCSR). Its 14-bit prescaler offers T1CK and T1CK/2 through T1CK/16384 in powers of two, or stop, selected by CS1[3:0]. PSR1 in TCCR1B resets the prescaler, to align the timer with program execution. To switch to asynchronous mode: enable the PLL, wait 100 µs for it to settle, poll PLOCK until it is set, then set PCKE.

Depending on the mode, the counter clears, counts up or counts down on each timer clock. With CS1[3:0] = 0 it stops, yet the CPU can still access TCNT1, and CPU writes win over clear and count. WGM1[1:0], PWM1A and PWM1B set the count sequence; TOV1 is set as the mode defines and can interrupt.

TCNT1 is compared with OCR1A to OCR1D; a match sets OCF1A, OCF1B or OCF1D on the next timer clock and can interrupt, the flag clearing when the interrupt runs or when one is written to it. The waveform generator uses the match with PWM1A, PWM1B, WGM1[1:0] and COM1x[1:0] to form its output. In every PWM mode OCR1x is double buffered and updated at TOP or BOTTOM, which keeps PWM pulses symmetrical and glitch-free; in normal mode the buffering is off. Between a write and the update, reading OCR1x returns the newly written value.

operation.topic: Timer/Counter1 force compare and write blocking
operation.text: In non-PWM modes, writing one to FOC1x updates the waveform output OCW1x as a match would (set, clear or toggle per COM1x[1:0]) without setting OCF1x or clearing the timer. A CPU write to TCNT1 blocks compare matches in the next timer clock even with the timer stopped, so writing TCNT1 equal to OCR1x loses that match and corrupts the waveform; nor should TCNT1 be written to BOTTOM while counting down. Set OCW1x before making the pin an output, most simply with FOC1x in normal mode; OC1x keeps its value across mode changes. COM1x[1:0] is not double buffered and acts at once.

Each of the three PWM channels has a dead-time generator that, in a PWM mode with COM1x[1:0] = 01, makes a non-overlapping complementary pair OC1x and ~OC1x from the waveform output, for driving external power switches safely. Its own prescaler, set by DTPS1[1:0], divides the PCK or CK timer clock by 1, 2, 4 or 8. On each edge of OCW1x a 4-bit down counter is loaded from DT1H or DT1L in register DT1 and holds back the rising edge of OC1x or ~OC1x until it reaches zero, so the two edges get separate dead times: DT1H sets the non-overlap at the rising edge, DT1L at the falling edge. With dead time set to zero the outputs still lag the waveform output by at least one timer clock. Setting PWM1X inverts both outputs, which then sit high during the dead time.

COM1x[1:0] sets whether the next match drives OCW1x inverted or not, and whether the OC1x and ~OC1x pins are driven. In normal mode the dead-time generator is off and only delays OC1x by one timer clock from OCW1x. In fast PWM and phase and frequency correct PWM with COM1x[1:0] = 01, both true and inverted outputs appear with programmable dead time; other settings behave as in normal mode. A system reset clears OC1x to 0. Setting either COM1x bit hands the port pin to the timer output, but the pin's DDR bit must still be set as an output before the value appears, which allows OC1x to be initialised before the pin is enabled. A COM1x change takes effect at the first match after the write; FOC1x makes it immediate in non-PWM modes. COM1x[1:0] = 0 means no action at the next match in every mode.
PWM1A, PWM1B and WGM1[1:0] set the count sequence; COM1x[1:0] only shapes the output (inverted, non-inverted or complementary in PWM modes; set, clear or toggle in non-PWM modes).

With PWM1A/PWM1B = 0 the counter runs from BOTTOM to TOP (OCR1C), clearing on the clock after the match, which sets resolution and output frequency. Toggle mode toggles OCW1x at each match with OCR1x; non-inverting mode clears it and inverting mode sets it. TOV1 sets as TCNT1 becomes zero, acting as an eleventh bit that is only set, so software can extend resolution with the overflow interrupt; the counter may be written at any time. Generating waveforms in normal mode is not recommended because it costs too much CPU time; toggle mode on OC1x gives at most fclkT1/4 with OCR1C = 0.

PWM1A/PWM1B = 1 with WGM1[1:0] = 00 gives single-slope PWM: the count runs from BOTTOM to TOP (OCR1C) and restarts. Non-inverting output (COM1x = 2) clears OCW1x on the match and sets it at BOTTOM; inverting output (COM1x = 3) does the opposite; complementary mode (COM1x = 1) clears on the match, sets at BOTTOM and drives both OC1x and ~OC1x. Single slope allows twice the frequency of the dual-slope mode, suiting power regulation, rectification and DAC uses with small external inductors and capacitors. TOV1 sets at each TOP and its handler can update the compare value. OCR1C = BOTTOM gives a narrow spike every MAX+1 timer clocks; OCR1C = MAX gives a constant high or low output. A 50% square wave at up to fclkT1/4 comes from toggling OCW1x (COM1x = 1) with OCR1C = 3. The pins show the timer outputs only when a COM1x bit is set and their DDR bits are outputs; otherwise the port value appears.

operation.topic: Phase and frequency correct PWM mode
operation.text: PWM1A/PWM1B = 1 with WGM1[1:0] = 01 gives dual-slope PWM: the count rises from BOTTOM to TOP (OCR1C), holds TOP for one timer clock and falls back. Non-inverting output clears OCW1x on the match while counting up and sets it on the match while counting down; inverting output does the reverse; complementary mode drives both OC1x and ~OC1x. Its top frequency is lower than single slope, but its symmetry suits motor control. TOV1 sets at each BOTTOM. With OCR1C = BOTTOM the non-inverted output stays low, and with OCR1C = MAX it stays high; inverted outputs take the opposite levels.

PWM1A = 1 with WGM1[1:0] = 1X drives all six outputs from the single waveform OCW1A set by OCR1A, for example for brushless DC motor control. The OC1OE bits in TCCR1E connect or release each pin at once: a cleared bit leaves the port value on the pin. WGM10 = 0 gives single-slope counting as in fast PWM (TOV1 at TOP); WGM10 = 1 gives dual-slope counting as in phase and frequency correct PWM (TOV1 at BOTTOM). In both, the TOV1 handler can update the compare value.

TOV1 sets as the count goes from TOP to BOTTOM in every mode but phase and frequency correct PWM, with or without the prescaler; OCF1x sets on the timer clock after TCNT1 equals OCR1x in every mode; in phase and frequency correct PWM, TOV1 sets as the count reaches BOTTOM.

Setting FPEN1 arms the unit, which is triggered by a level change on INT0 or, with FPAC1 in TCCR1D set, by the analog comparator output. On a trigger the COM1x bits clear, the compare outputs leave the PWM pins and the PORTB bits drive them instead, and FPEN1 clears on the same system clock. With FPIE1 set a fault protection interrupt is raised; otherwise software can poll FPEN1. Changing the trigger source, the edge or enabling the unit can itself trigger it, so clear FPF1 after any of these. The inputs are sampled like T0; the noise canceler (FPNC1) passes a change only after four equal samples, adding four system clocks of delay, and runs from the system clock regardless of the prescaler. Driving the INT0 port bit from software can trigger it.

Through the shared TC1H register, write the high bits to TC1H before writing the low byte, and read the low byte before TC1H; each low-byte access moves both parts in one clock. Since an interrupt that touches any 10-bit timer register changes TC1H, main code should disable interrupts around such accesses when handlers use these registers too. When several registers share the same high bits, TC1H need only be written once.

The universal serial interface gives the hardware for serial links with little software: two-wire (master or slave) and three-wire (master or slave) synchronous transfers, a data-received interrupt, wake-up from idle, and in two-wire mode wake-up from every sleep mode including power-down through a start condition detector with its own interrupt. USIDR is an unbuffered 8-bit shift register, so received data must be read promptly. Its MSB feeds DO or SDA through a transparent latch that changes the output on the clock edge opposite the sampling edge; serial input is always taken from DI. A 4-bit counter, readable and writable, is clocked with the data register and overflows at the end of a transfer; with an external clock it counts both edges. The clock comes from USCK, the Timer/Counter0 compare match, or software. In two-wire mode the clock control unit can interrupt on a start condition and hold the clock low after a start or a counter overflow to insert wait states.

Compatible with SPI modes 0 and 1 but without a slave select pin, which software can supply; pins DI, DO and USCK. After eight USCK clocks two connected USI data registers have swapped contents, and USIOIF marks completion. The master makes the clock by toggling USCK through PORT or by writing one to USITC. In external clock mode 0 (USICS0 = 0) DI is sampled on rising edges and DO changes on falling edges; mode 1 uses the opposite edges. Both sides load USIDR and set their output's DDR bit at least half a USCK cycle before the first sampling edge, and the counter is reset; each clock pulse is two edges, so the counter overflows after eight pulses (16 edges), and the overflow interrupt can wake the CPU from idle. A size-optimised master routine shifts one byte in a loop strobing USITC; an unrolled one reaches fSCK = fCK/2. A slave routine sets three-wire mode with an external positive-edge clock and waits on USIOIF; it needs DO as output and USCK as input.

Compatible with the TWI (I2C) protocol but with no slew-rate limiting on outputs and no input noise filtering; pins SCL and SDA. Only the physical layer is in hardware: the master generates SCL in software by toggling USCK through PORTA, the shifting is automatic, and shifting on negative edges is the practical choice. The slave can insert wait states by holding SCL low, so the master must check that SCL was really released after each rising edge. The counter overflow marks the end of a transfer. A protocol such as TWI decides the data direction.

The master makes a start condition by pulling SDA low while SCL is high, by writing zero to USIDR bit 7 or to the PORTA bit, with the DDR bit set. The slave's start detector sets USISIF, which can interrupt, and holds SCL low after the master's falling SCL edge until the slave clears the flag and resets the counter. The master then puts out each bit and releases SCL; the slave samples on rising SCL. After eight bits (address and R/W) the slave counter overflows and pulls SCL low; a slave not addressed releases SCL and waits for the next start. An addressed slave holds SDA low for the acknowledge, by setting the counter to 14 before releasing SCL, and may hold SCL low again after it. Bytes then flow in one direction until a stop or a new start. A slave that cannot take more data leaves the last byte unacknowledged; a master ending a read forces the acknowledge bit after the last byte.

Works only in two-wire mode. SDA is delayed by 50 ns to 300 ns so that SCL is sampled validly. Being asynchronous, it can wake the part from power-down, but the SCL hold time the protocol allows must then cover the oscillator start-up chosen with the CKSEL fuses.

SCL and SCK run at most at fCK/2, which is also the top data rate in both two- and three-wire modes. In two-wire slave mode the clock control unit holds SCL low until the slave is ready, which can lower the real data rate.

With no serial link to serve, the USI can act as a half-duplex asynchronous data port (a UART more compact and faster than software alone) using USIDR in three-wire mode; a stand-alone 4-bit counter with overflow interrupt, counting both edges when clocked externally; a 12-bit counter together with an 8-bit timer; an extra edge-triggered external interrupt, by loading the counter with 0xF and using the overflow flag and enable, selected with USICS1; or a software interrupt fired by strobing the clock.

USIDR is accessed directly; depending on USICS[1:0] it shifts left on an external clock edge, a Timer/Counter0 compare match or the USICLK strobe. A serial clock in the same cycle as a write leaves the written value unshifted. Even with no wire mode selected (USIWM[1:0] = 0), DI/SDA and USCK/SCL can still feed USIDR. The output latch is open during the first half of each serial clock with an external clock (USICS1 = 1) and always open with an internal clock (USICS1 = 0); while it is open, a new MSB appears on the pin at once. The output pin's DDR bit must be set for data to leave the register.

Compares a positive input chosen from AIN0, AIN1 or AIN2 with a negative input chosen from the same pins, and sets ACO when the positive input is higher. It has its own interrupt, on a rising, falling or toggling output. The bandgap reference can replace an input (ACBG). With the ADC switched off (ADEN = 0) and ACME in ADCSRB set, MUX[5:0] in ADMUX selects any of ADC0 to ADC10 as the negative input; with ACME cleared or ADEN set, ACM[2:0] picks among AIN0 to AIN2.

A 10-bit successive-approximation converter: integral non-linearity 1.0 LSB, absolute accuracy ±2 LSB, conversion in 13 µs, and up to 15 kSPS at full resolution. An analog multiplexer offers 11 single-ended inputs on PA[7:0] and PB[7:4] referred to GND, 16 differential pairs (15 with selectable gain of 1x, 8x, 20x or 32x), and a temperature sensor channel. The input range is 0 to VCC. References are VCC (single-ended channels), an external voltage on AREF (PA3), or internal 1.1 V or 2.56 V, the 2.56 V optionally decoupled by a capacitor on AREF for lower noise; REFS[2:0] in ADCSRB and ADMUX choose. Other features: optional left-adjusted result, free-running or single conversion, auto triggering from interrupt sources, a conversion-complete interrupt, a sleep-mode noise canceler, unipolar or bipolar input mode and input polarity reversal. A sample-and-hold keeps the input steady during conversion.

MUX[5:0] in ADMUX choose the channel and gain; GSEL in ADCSRB also takes part in the gain choice. On a differential channel the gain stage amplifies the difference by the selected factor; single-ended channels bypass it. Selecting the same pin as both inputs measures the remaining offset of the gain stage and converter, which can be subtracted from later results at the same gain to bring offset below 1 LSB. MUX = 111111 selects the temperature sensor on channel ADC11. ADEN in ADCSRA turns the ADC on; reference and channel choices take effect only then, and with ADEN cleared it draws no power, so turning it off before power-saving sleep is recommended. The result sits in ADCH and ADCL, right-adjusted unless ADLAR is set. For 8 bits from a left-adjusted result, reading ADCH alone is enough; otherwise read ADCL first, then ADCH. Reading ADCL locks both registers until ADCH is read, so a conversion that finishes in between is lost, though its interrupt still fires.

Writing one to ADSC starts a single conversion; ADSC stays one until it ends. A channel change during a conversion waits until that conversion completes. With ADATE set, a rising edge on the source chosen by ADTS in ADCSRB resets the prescaler and starts a conversion, giving fixed-interval sampling; if the trigger is still high when the conversion ends, or a second edge arrives during it, no extra conversion starts. The trigger's interrupt flag sets even when its interrupt is disabled, and must be cleared before the next event can trigger. Using ADIF as the trigger gives free-running mode, where a new conversion starts as each ends whether or not ADIF is cleared; the first must be started by writing ADSC. ADSC reads one during any conversion, however started, and can start single conversions in auto-trigger mode.

Full 10-bit resolution needs an ADC clock between 50 kHz and 200 kHz; lower resolution permits a faster clock and higher sample rate. A 7-bit prescaler divides the CPU clock (above 100 kHz) by 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128 as set by ADPS in ADCSRA; it runs while ADEN is set and is held in reset while ADEN is low. A single conversion begins on the next rising ADC clock after ADSC is set. A normal conversion lasts 13 ADC clocks with sample-and-hold 1.5 clocks in; the first after enabling lasts 25 clocks, sample-and-hold at 13.5, to initialise the analog circuitry. On completion the result is written, ADIF sets and, in single conversion mode, ADSC clears. With auto triggering the prescaler resets on the trigger, sample-and-hold falls two ADC clocks after the trigger edge, and three CPU clocks go to synchronization. In free-running mode the next conversion starts immediately while ADSC stays high.

MUX[5:0] and REFS[2:0] pass through a temporary register, so changes take effect only at a safe moment: they update continuously until a conversion starts, are locked during it, and resume updating in the last ADC clock before it ends (ADIF set). Because a conversion starts on the ADC clock after ADSC is written, wait one ADC clock after writing ADSC before writing new selections. With ADATE and ADEN both set, a trigger can come at any time, so a change cannot be tied to a conversion; ADMUX is safe to update while ADATE or ADEN is cleared, during a conversion at least one ADC clock after the trigger, or after a conversion before clearing the flag used as trigger. In single conversion mode select the channel before starting; in free-running mode select it before the first conversion and expect the result after a change to reflect the old channel once, since the next conversion has already begun.

VREF sets the conversion range; single-ended inputs above it read close to 0x3FF. VREF can be VCC, the internal 1.1 V or 2.56 V, or the AREF pin. Discard the first result after switching the reference source, which may be inaccurate.

Conversions can run during ADC noise reduction or idle sleep to cut noise from the CPU and peripherals. With the ADC enabled and idle, single conversion mode selected and the conversion-complete interrupt enabled, entering the sleep mode starts a conversion once the CPU halts; the ADC interrupt then wakes the CPU. If another interrupt wakes it first, that one runs and the ADC interrupt follows at completion, the CPU staying active until the next SLEEP. Other sleep modes do not turn the ADC off, so clear ADEN before entering them to avoid excess current.

Each ADCn pin carries its pin capacitance and leakage whether or not it is selected. When selected, the source charges the sample-and-hold capacitance, 14 pF worst case including stray capacitance, through a series resistance of 1 kΩ to 100 kΩ. Sources of about 10 kΩ or less make sampling time negligible; higher-impedance sources need longer, so low-impedance sources and slowly varying signals are recommended. Remove signal content above the Nyquist frequency (fADC/2) with a low-pass filter before the input.

Keep analog paths short and over the analog ground plane, away from fast digital tracks; do not switch port pins used as digital outputs during a conversion; fit bypass capacitors right at the VCC and GND pins. ADC noise reduction mode is recommended where accuracy matters, especially above 1 MHz system clock or when reading the temperature sensor; good external bypassing reduces the need for it.

An n-bit single-ended ADC divides GND to VREF into 2^n steps, reading 0 to 2^n - 1. Offset: deviation of the first transition (0x000 to 0x001) from its ideal at 0.5 LSB. Gain error: after removing offset, deviation of the last transition (0x3FE to 0x3FF) from its ideal 1.5 LSB below full scale. Integral non-linearity: after removing offset and gain error, the largest deviation of any transition from ideal. Differential non-linearity: the largest deviation of a code width from 1 LSB. The ideal for each of these is 0 LSB. Quantization error is always ±0.5 LSB. Absolute accuracy: the largest deviation of any unadjusted transition from ideal, combining all the above; ideal ±0.5 LSB.

After ADIF sets, ADCL and ADCH hold the result in one of three forms. Single-ended: one-sided, 0x000 to 0x3FF. Unipolar differential: one-sided, the positive input needing to stay above the negative or the result saturates at zero. Bipolar differential (BIN in ADCSRB set): two's complement, allowing either input to be higher. A signal that is not truly bipolar loses one bit of range in bipolar mode; checking the sign (ADC9 in ADCH: one is negative) and then converting the pair unipolar in the right polarity keeps the full range.

The on-chip sensor sits on single-ended channel ADC11, enabled by MUX[5:0] = 111111, and needs the internal 1.1 V reference; it is read in single conversion mode. Its output is linear with temperature, about 1 LSB per °C. After a single-point calibration at room temperature accuracy is typically ±10 °C; two-point calibration does better.

A one-wire bidirectional on-chip debug interface that controls program flow, executes AVR instructions in the CPU and programs the non-volatile memories. It emulates all on-chip functions, digital and analog, except the RESET pin; runs in real time, non-intrusively, with the part's own electrical characteristics; and supports unlimited software breakpoints and symbolic debugging. Programming DWEN with the lock bits unprogrammed turns it on and makes RESET an open-drain bidirectional I/O with pull-up, the link to the emulator. The system clock stays as chosen by the CKSEL fuses.

A breakpoint replaces an instruction in Flash with BREAK, the original being kept and executed on resume; BREAK can also be placed by hand. Each breakpoint change reprograms Flash, which shortens its data retention, so parts used for debugging should not be shipped. With dW on the RESET pin, external reset is not available. I/O is emulated exactly while the CPU runs; with the CPU stopped, some I/O registers need care when accessed through the debugger. The link is asynchronous, so a software clock change (CLKPS) may break communication, and clocks below 100 kHz may cause trouble. A programmed DWEN keeps parts of the clock system running in every sleep mode, raising sleep current, so DWEN should be unprogrammed when debugWIRE is not in use. DWDR passes data from the running program to the debugger and is reachable only through debugWIRE.

The MCU can load and store its own program code over any data interface. SPM is disabled until the SELFPRGEN fuse is programmed (0); there is no separate boot section, so SPM then covers the whole Flash. Flash is written a page at a time: each page is erased before being written from the temporary page buffer, which is filled a word at a time with SPM either before erasing or between erase and write. To change part of a page, save the rest (for example in the buffer) before erasing and write it back; filling first allows read-modify-write, filling after erase does not. The buffer can be filled in any order. Page erase and page write must address the same page.

Page erase: page address in the Z pointer (PCPAGE), 00000011 into SPMCSR, then SPM no more than four clocks later; R1:R0 are ignored and the CPU halts during the erase. Page load: address in Z, word in R1:R0, 00000001 into SPMCSR, then SPM no more than four clocks later; PCWORD selects the buffer word. Each buffer address can be written only once before the buffer is erased, which happens after a page write, on writing CTPB in SPMCSR, or on reset. An EEPROM write during page loading loses all loaded data. Page write: page address in PCPAGE, other Z bits zero, 00000101 into SPMCSR, then SPM no more than four clocks later; the CPU halts during the write. In Z, the low bits pick the word inside a page and the high bits pick which page; LPM addresses bytes, so it also uses Z0.
While an EEPROM write is in progress, software programming of Flash and software reads of fuses and lock bits are blocked. Check that EEPE in EECR is clear before writing SPMCSR.

operation.topic: Reading fuse and lock bits from software
operation.text: Firmware can read the fuse and lock bits; programmed bits read as 0 and unprogrammed bits as 1. Load Z, set RFLB and SELFPRGEN in SPMCSR, and issue LPM within three CPU cycles; the byte lands in the LPM destination register. RFLB and SELFPRGEN clear when the read completes, or if no LPM follows within three cycles or no SPM within four, after which LPM works normally. Z = 0x0001 returns the lock bits (LB2 in bit 1, LB1 in bit 0); Z = 0x0000 the fuse low byte; Z = 0x0003 the fuse high byte; Z = 0x0002 the fuse extended byte.

At too low a VCC, Flash writes may fail and the CPU may execute instructions wrongly. Either of two measures avoids corruption: hold RESET active through periods of low supply, using the internal brown-out detector where its level suits the operating voltage or an external low-VCC reset otherwise (a write in progress at reset completes if the supply is sufficient); or keep the core in power-down sleep while VCC is low, so no instruction can write SPMCSR.
Flash accesses from the CPU are timed by the calibrated internal oscillator.

Two lock bits, unprogrammed (1) or programmed (0), add the protection of the lock modes; only a chip erase returns them to 1. Flash can still be read out through debugWIRE with DWEN programmed even when lock bits are set, so DWEN should be cleared when lock-bit security is needed. Firmware can read the lock bits.

Three fuse bytes: extended, high and low. Programmed fuses read as 0. Programming LB1 locks the fuse bits, so program fuses before lock bits; a chip erase does not change fuses. Fuse values are latched on entering programming mode and on power-up, and changes act only after programming mode is left, except EESAVE, which acts as soon as it is programmed.

A three-byte signature in its own address space identifies the device and can be read in serial and high-voltage programming modes, even when locked. The signature area also holds one calibration byte for the internal oscillator, in the high byte of address 0x000, copied into OSCCAL during reset.

Flash and EEPROM can be programmed over SPI (SCK, MOSI in, MISO out) while RESET is held at GND; the Programming Enable instruction must be sent first. In serial mode an EEPROM write erases the location itself, so no chip erase is needed; a chip erase sets every Flash and EEPROM location to 0xFF. A valid clock is needed as set by the CKSEL fuses. SCK low and high periods must each exceed 2 CPU clocks below 12 MHz and 3 CPU clocks at 12 MHz or more. Data into the part is clocked on SCK's rising edge, data out on its falling edge.

Power up with RESET and SCK at 0; if SCK cannot be held low during power-up, pulse RESET high for at least tRST plus two CPU clocks once SCK is 0. Wait at least 20 ms and send Programming Enable on MOSI. When in step, the second byte (0x53) echoes back while the third is sent; all four bytes are always sent, and if the echo is missing, pulse RESET and try again. Flash is written a page at a time: load each byte with Load Program Memory Page and the address's low bits (low byte before high byte for each address), then store that page with Write Program Memory Page and the high address bits; without RDY/BSY polling wait at least tWD_FLASH before the next page, since earlier access can corrupt the write. EEPROM can be written byte by byte (each location erased automatically, wait tWD_EEPROM between bytes) or a page at a time (load bytes with Load EEPROM Memory Page and the 2 low address bits, store with Write EEPROM Memory Page; only loaded locations change). After a chip erase, 0xFF data need not be written. Read instructions return any location on MISO for verification. Setting RESET high ends programming and starts normal operation; to power off, set RESET to 1 and then remove VCC.

High-voltage parallel programming writes and verifies Flash, EEPROM, lock bits and fuse bits. Pulses are at least 250 ns long unless stated otherwise. XA1 and XA0 choose what a positive XTAL1 pulse does; pulsing WR or OE executes the loaded command.

Apply 4.5 V to 5.5 V between VCC and GND. Hold RESET at 0 and toggle XTAL1 at least six times. Set the Prog_enable pins to 0000 and wait at least 100 ns. Apply 11.5 V to 12.5 V to RESET; any change on the Prog_enable pins within 100 ns after the 12 V is applied makes entry fail. Wait at least 50 µs before the next command.

Command and address are kept during programming, so a command is loaded once for many locations; 0xFF data need not be written after a chip erase (to the EEPROM too, unless EESAVE is programmed); the address high byte is loaded only when moving to a new 256-word Flash or 256-byte EEPROM window, and likewise for signature reads.

Erases Flash, EEPROM and lock bits, the lock bits only after the Flash is fully erased; fuses are unchanged. A chip erase is required before reprogramming Flash or EEPROM, and EESAVE preserves the EEPROM. Load command 1000 0000 (XA1:XA0 = 10, BS1 = 0, pulse XTAL1), pulse WR low to start, then let RDY/BSY return high before loading another command.

Load command 0001 0000. For each word: load the address low byte (XA1:XA0 = 00, BS1 = 0), the data low byte (XA1:XA0 = 01) and the data high byte (BS1 = 1), each with an XTAL1 pulse, until the buffer is full. Then load the address high byte (XA1:XA0 = 00, BS1 = 1), pulse WR low to write it all and wait until RDY/BSY is high again. Repeat for every page, then load command 0000 0000 (no operation) to reset the internal write signals. The low address bits select the word inside a page and the high bits select which page; with fewer than 256 words per page, the top bits of the address low byte also help pick which page.

Load command 0001 0001 and the address high byte; for each byte load the address low byte and the data, then latch it with a positive PAGEL pulse, until the buffer is full. With BS1 at 0, a low pulse on WR programs that page; RDY/BSY returns high before the next one may start.

operation.topic: Parallel reading of Flash and EEPROM
operation.text: Flash: load command 0000 0010 and the address high and low bytes; with OE = 0 and BS1 = 0 the word's low byte is on DATA, with BS1 = 1 its high byte; then set OE to 1. EEPROM: load command 0000 0011 and the address bytes; with OE = 0 and BS1 = 0 the byte is on DATA; then set OE to 1.

Load command 0100 0000 and the data low byte (bit = 0 programs a fuse, 1 erases it). For the low byte pulse WR directly; for the high byte set BS1 = 1, BS2 = 0 first; for the extended byte set BS1 = 0, BS2 = 1 first; then wait for RDY/BSY to go high and return BS1 or BS2 to 0. Lock bits: load command 0010 0000, then the data low byte (0 programs a bit), pulse WR and wait for RDY/BSY. Only a chip erase clears lock bits; with LB mode 3 the boot lock bits cannot be programmed by any external programming mode.

operation.topic: Parallel reading of fuses, lock, signature and calibration
operation.text: Load command 0000 0100, set OE = 0 and choose the byte with BS2 and BS1 (programmed bits read 0), then set OE to 1. Signature bytes: load command 0000 1000 and address low byte 0x00 to 0x02; with OE = 0 and BS1 = 0 the byte is on DATA. Calibration byte: same command, address 0x00, OE = 0 and BS1 = 1.
The highest operating frequency depends on VCC and is piecewise linear between three points: 4 MHz at 1.8 V, 10 MHz at 2.7 V and 20 MHz at 4.5 V, staying at 20 MHz up to 5.5 V.
The internal oscillator can be calibrated by the user more closely than the factory calibration. Its frequency moves with temperature and voltage.

In serial programming MOSI is set up before and held after the rising edge of SCK, where the device samples it; MISO becomes valid a time tSLIV after the falling edge of SCK. Bytes are shifted most significant bit first.

Data and control lines (DATA, XA0, XA1/BS2, PAGEL/BS1) are set up before and held after each XTAL1 pulse; tDVXH, tXHXL and tXLDX apply to loading and to reading. A write starts on the WR low pulse and RDY/BSY goes low then returns high when the write is done. Reading within a page: after the address is loaded, OE low puts the data byte on DATA, BS1 choosing the low or the high byte, and OE high returns DATA to high impedance.

The typical curves come largely from simulation and from characterisation of similar devices made in the same process; they show typical behaviour and are not production-tested. Devices were run above their test frequencies during characterisation, but operation above the frequency of the ordering code is not guaranteed. Supply currents were measured with every I/O pin an input with its pull-up on, clocked from a rail-to-rail sine generator. Power-down current does not depend on the clock source. The watchdog timer's own current is the difference between power-down current with the watchdog on and with it off. Supply current depends mostly on supply voltage and frequency, and also on I/O loading and switching, the code run and the ambient temperature.

ATtiny261A: revision D has no known errata; revision C was not sampled. ATtiny461A: revision C has no known errata. ATtiny861A: revision D has no known errata; revision C was not sampled. The revision letter is the device's silicon revision.
